items.prompt: Approving a design after a quick skim, with no real questions, is called what?
items.explanation: Rubber-stamping means approving without engaging with the design itself.

items.prompt: Eleven comments, nine about naming and formatting, is an example of what?
items.explanation: Nitpicking engages only with the cheap, safe-to-comment parts.

items.prompt: What is a design review mainly meant to catch?
items.explanation: The point is finding expensive mistakes while they are still cheap to change on paper.

items.prompt: Which review comment is most likely to make the design safer?
items.explanation: Only the failure-mode question tests a real risk.

items.prompt: Both failure modes avoid which kind of work?
choices: Forming an opinion on the design
items.explanation: Each one skips judging whether the design will hold up.

items.prompt: Which review style feels efficient and friendly but tests nothing?
items.explanation: Fast agreement is pleasant, which is why it is tempting.

items.prompt: Which review style looks rigorous because of its comment count?
items.explanation: A large count makes it look thorough while the design stays untested.

items.prompt: A review is not mainly a test of what?
items.explanation: Review judges the design, not the person who wrote it.

items.prompt: A reviewer says 'I left 14 comments, so I clearly took this seriously.' Every comment concerns wording. What is the flaw in that reasoning?
choices: Comment count does not measure whether risk was tested
Fourteen comments is far too many for a single design document
Wording comments belong in the chat thread rather than the doc
Serious reviews avoid commenting on wording of any kind at all
items.explanation: Counting comments measures effort, not coverage. A review earns its keep by testing the decisions that are costly to reverse, and wording comments do not touch them.
items.reference:
Two ways to miss the design
👍 rubber-stamp: approve without testing
🔤 nitpick: comment only on surface details
🎯 substantive: test the costly decisions
🧪 test: would addressing every comment make it safer?
Why: both failure modes avoid forming an opinion on whether the design holds up.
items.learnMore:
Volume of comments is not depth of review

A review is useful to the degree its comments change the risk in the design. Two LGTMs and eleven naming comments can both leave the same failure mode untouched.

Common mistake

Counting comments as a measure of rigor, when a spell-checker could have made most of them.
items.reflection: Think of a time you checked someone's work, a form, a plan or a trip itinerary. Did you check the parts that were easy to check or the parts that could actually fail?

items.prompt: A well-known author's doc gets one reply, 'looks good, you know this area better than I do.' Which failure mode is that, and why?
choices: Nitpicking: the reply is far too short to be genuinely useful
Rubber-stamping: deference replaced testing the design
Substantive review: trusting an expert is the efficient approach
Neither one: a reply that polite cannot possibly be a failure
items.explanation: Deferring to expertise replaces the testing the review exists for. Looking friendly and efficient is exactly why rubber-stamping persists.

choices: The second is better because it has more comments
The first is better because shorter reviews are focused
None: counts alone do not show which tested real risks
Both are equal since each one found something
items.explanation: Counts say nothing about content. Only reading what each comment tests, and whether addressing it would make the design safer, separates the two.

items.prompt: What exact question separates a useful review from a failed one, per the unit's test?
choices: Did the reviewer finish writing before the meeting started?
Did the author reply to each of the comments politely enough?
Were the comments grouped by the section of the doc they sit in?
Would the design be safer if every comment were addressed?
items.explanation: The unit's test ties a review's value to the change in the design: if addressing every comment leaves it no safer, cheaper or more reliable, the review failed.

items.prompt: Which category asks what happens when a component is down or slow?
items.explanation: This question probes how far a failure spreads.

items.prompt: Which category asks whether the design holds at 10x traffic?
items.explanation: Scale questions test the design above and below the demoed size.

items.prompt: Which category asks what else was considered?
items.explanation: A trade-off question compares the choice against other options.

items.prompt: Which category asks how hard it is to undo in six months?
items.explanation: Reversibility measures the cost of being wrong.

items.prompt: Which category asks who gets paged when it breaks?
items.explanation: Ownership covers who runs and debugs the system.

items.prompt: How many categories make up the fixed set?
items.explanation: The unit uses the same five on every doc.

items.prompt: Does the set of categories change depending on what the doc emphasizes?
items.explanation: A fixed set avoids steering by the author's emphasis.

items.prompt: What do the categories protect a reviewer from doing?
choices: Reacting only to what catches the eye
Asking any questions about the design
items.explanation: Without them, attention drifts to surface details.

items.prompt: A doc argues at length for its chosen queue but never mentions any other option. Which category exposes the gap?
items.explanation: Asking what else was considered is the trade-offs category. A doc that argues for one option without comparing any is exactly what it catches.
items.reference:
Five questions, every doc
📈 scale and load: 10x and a tenth
💥 failure modes: what if it is down or slow
⚖️ trade-offs: what else was considered
↩️ reversibility: how hard to undo in six months
🔧 operability: who gets paged and can they debug it
Why: a fixed set of categories pulls the review onto the design instead of whatever catches the eye.
items.learnMore:
A checklist beats reacting to the page

Because the categories are the same for every doc, the review is not steered by what the author chose to emphasize. A doc silent on failure modes still gets the failure-mode question.

Common mistake

Only asking about the categories the doc already discusses, which lets its blind spots through.
items.reflection: Pick a decision outside software, such as buying a car or moving cities. Which of the five questions would you have skipped if you had only reacted to the brochure?

items.prompt: A design is demoed with 50 users and works. Which category asks the question that demo cannot answer?

Scale and load: behavior at 10x and at a tenth
Operability: who attended the demo meeting last week
Trade-offs: which demo software the team picked to use
items.explanation: A demo at one size says nothing about 10x or a tenth. The scale category asks the question the demo cannot answer.

items.prompt: A comment about naming a variable differently is usually what severity?
items.explanation: A naming preference costs nothing to skip.

items.prompt: A missing failure-mode analysis for a critical path is usually what?
items.explanation: A real unexamined risk must be resolved first.

items.prompt: The reviewer honestly does not know and asks. Which severity fits?
items.explanation: A question marks a gap in the reviewer's knowledge that the doc should fill.

items.prompt: Which severity is optional and costs nothing to skip?
items.explanation: Nits are marked optional so they never pose as more.

items.prompt: Which severity must be resolved before the design moves forward?
items.explanation: Blocking items gate the design.

items.prompt: A review with nothing blocking, should-fix, or question is which failure mode?
items.explanation: Nothing real was raised.

items.prompt: A review where every comment is a nit is which failure mode?
items.explanation: Everything landed in the least important row.

items.prompt: Why label comments by severity at all?
choices: So the review looks a good deal longer
So not everything reads as equally urgent
So the author feels free to skip every note
So the meeting can be shortened by a lot
items.explanation: Labels tell the author what each comment requires.

items.prompt: A doc proposes no rollback for a one-way database change. The reviewer writes 'might be worth thinking about'. What is wrong?
choices: A blocking-level risk is wrapped in soft tone and no label
Rollback plans count as a nit under every possible reading
The comment is too long to qualify for a should-fix label
Database changes sit outside the scope of any design review
items.explanation: A one-way change with no rollback is a real risk, so it blocks. Soft wording with no label leaves the author unsure it matters.
items.reference:
Four labels, four weights
🛑 blocking: real risk, resolve before moving on
🔧 should-fix: improves it, would not block alone
❓ question: reviewer truly does not know
🪶 nit: preference, optional to skip
Why: labels stop a naming preference from reading as urgent as a missing failure analysis.
items.learnMore:
Severity is a promise about what happens next

A blocking label tells the author the design cannot proceed. A nit label tells them it can. If everything has the same weight the author has to guess, and usually guesses wrong.

Common mistake

Using question as a polite way to hide a blocking concern you already have an answer to.
items.reflection: When you give someone feedback, outside of work, do you signal which parts are must-fix and which are taste? What happens when you do not?

items.prompt: A reviewer has a real concern about queue ordering but writes 'Question: is this ordered?' while already knowing it is not. Why is that a problem?
choices: Questions are never permitted anywhere in a design review
It disguises a finding as a question the author can dodge
It should have carried the nit label because it was brief
The author is unable to answer questions about ordering
items.explanation: A question should mark real ignorance. Using it to hide a finding lets the author treat a required fix as optional.

items.prompt: What should a reviewer do before leaving any comment?
items.explanation: The full read forms an opinion of the whole design first.

items.prompt: What is listed right after reading the doc?
items.explanation: Claims give the review a list of things to test.

items.prompt: A load-bearing claim is one the design does what?
items.explanation: If the claim is wrong, the design is wrong.

items.prompt: Which step comes before sorting by severity?
items.explanation: Findings are produced by the testing step.

items.prompt: In what order should findings be delivered?
choices: In the order they were noticed
items.explanation: Important items should not be buried.

items.prompt: How should nits be labeled when delivered?
items.explanation: Labeling them optional keeps them from posing as more.

items.prompt: Commenting while still reading mostly leads to comments on what?
items.explanation: Surface details are what is cheap to notice mid-read.

items.prompt: Which is a load-bearing claim?
items.explanation: It is a statement the design leans on.

items.prompt: A reviewer comments on every paragraph as they read and finishes with 20 notes, none on failure handling. What went wrong in the flow?
choices: Commenting during the read spent attention before claims appeared
They should have posted fewer than twenty notes in the end, since twenty is simply excessive
They sorted every note by severity before they had finished reading the doc
They delivered the blocking items ahead of the minor ones in the final message
items.explanation: Commenting while reading spends attention on whatever appears first, which is surface detail. The claims that matter only show up once the whole doc is read.
items.reference:
The order of work
📖 read it all once, no comments
🏗️ list the load-bearing claims
🧪 test each against the five categories
🗂️ sort by severity
📬 blocking first, nits last
Why: commenting while reading steers attention to whatever is cheap to notice.
items.learnMore:
A load-bearing claim is a place the design leans

Claims like 'no orders are lost' or 'each event is processed independently' hold up the rest of the design. Finding them first gives the review a list of things worth testing.

Common mistake

Treating every sentence as equally important instead of listing the few that carry weight.
items.reflection: When you proofread something important, do you read once for the whole picture first, or fix things as you go? What do you miss when you fix as you go?

items.prompt: Which sentence in a doc is the better candidate for a load-bearing claim?
choices: 'This document was last edited on a Tuesday afternoon'
'Consumers process events independently of each other'
'The diagram below shows how the services connect up'
'Section three is where the rollout plan is described'
items.explanation: A statement the rest of the design leans on, such as independent processing, is a claim worth testing. The others are navigation or housekeeping.

Send them in whichever order they appear inside the doc
Sort them by severity and lead with the blocking ones
Merge them all into a single summary comment at the end
items.explanation: Sorting by severity and leading with blocking items keeps the important findings from being buried under the rest.

items.prompt: Why does the flow have a separate step for listing claims instead of going straight to comments?

It makes the five question categories unnecessary to use
It gives the testing step a short list worth examining
items.explanation: Listing claims first turns a long doc into a short set of things to test, so the review spends effort where the design is actually leaning.

items.prompt: At which stage is changing a design decision cheapest?
items.explanation: On paper nothing has been built around it.

items.prompt: At which stage is changing a design decision costliest?
items.explanation: A change there needs a migration and a rollback plan.

items.prompt: The flaw is the same at every stage. What differs?
choices: The name the flaw is given
The person who wrote it down
How much is built around it
items.explanation: Cost grows with what depends on the wrong assumption.

items.prompt: Which stage comes right after doc review in the unit's ordering?
items.explanation: The ordering runs doc, prototype, mid-implementation, production.

items.prompt: Changing a design in a doc usually means what?
items.explanation: Nothing exists yet but the text.

items.prompt: Does the unit's cost ordering claim exact measured numbers?
choices: No, it is a qualitative ordering
items.explanation: It shows ordering, not measurements.

items.prompt: Why does design review exist, economically?
choices: It is required by company law
It is the cheapest point to be wrong
items.explanation: Mistakes cost least on paper.

items.prompt: Mid-implementation, a wrong design means rewriting what?
choices: Only the page of the doc
Only the diagram in the doc
Only the title of the doc
Code and the work built on it
items.explanation: Dependent work has to change too.

items.prompt: A team skips design review and plans to 'fix it in code review'. Why does that not recover the cheap-change window?
choices: The wrong assumption is already built into code
Code review is not permitted to request any design changes at all
Code reviewers are unable to open or read the design docs at all
Code review adds more meeting time than a design review ever does
items.explanation: Code review happens after the assumption is built in. The cheap window was the doc stage, when changing the design meant editing a page.
items.reference:
Where the same flaw gets caught
📝 doc review: edit a page
🧪 prototype: rework a throwaway
🏗️ mid-build: rewrite code and dependents
🏭 production: migrate with a rollback plan
Why: the flaw is identical at every stage; what grows is how much is built around it.
items.learnMore:
Review is the cheapest place to be wrong

At the doc stage changing 'event queue' back to 'direct call' is an edit. Later it is a rewrite, and in production it is a migration done when the flaw demands, not when the team chooses.

Common mistake

Believing code review will catch design flaws; by then the design is already poured into code.
items.reflection: Think of a plan you changed late, such as a trip or a renovation. What got more expensive to change as time passed, and what stayed free?

items.prompt: Two teams discover the same flaw: one in the doc, one in production. What is true?
choices: The production flaw is a different kind of flaw altogether
The flaw is the same; the cost to fix differs greatly
The doc flaw cost less because the flaw itself was smaller
The costs are equal whenever one person fixes both of them
items.explanation: The flaw does not change with the stage; what changes is how much depends on it. That is why the same flaw costs more later.

items.prompt: 'Events are retained for 7 days.' What does this describe?
items.explanation: It says the data survives, not how it is processed.

items.prompt: At-least-once delivery means an event may be processed how?
items.explanation: The same event can arrive again after a failure.

items.prompt: What customer-visible effect can at-least-once delivery cause?
items.explanation: Reprocessing repeats the send.

items.prompt: 'Removes the latency entirely' is true for which part?
items.explanation: Delivery still happens, just later.

items.prompt: Which category fits 'single deploy, cut over, done'?
items.explanation: It leaves rollback and in-flight orders unsaid.

items.prompt: What word names a send that is safe to repeat?
items.explanation: Repeating it gives the same result.

items.prompt: Retention answers 'is the data kept?' What does it not answer?
items.explanation: Keeping data is different from handling it.

items.prompt: What is a poison pill in a queue?
choices: An event that is very old
An event that is very large
items.explanation: It can stall everything behind it.

items.prompt: The doc says 'no orders are lost' because events are retained for 7 days. What is the sharper review question?
choices: Is each event processed at least once, and is a duplicate acceptable?
How many days of retention would be the right setting to choose?
Which cloud region should be used to store the retained events?
Why is the topic named with the word events at the end of it?
items.explanation: Retention is durability, not delivery. The sharper question is how many times each event is processed and whether a duplicate is acceptable.
items.reference:
Three claims, three gaps
📦 'removes latency': true for checkout only
🗄️ 'no orders lost': durability, not delivery
🚀 'drop-in, single deploy': no rollback stated
🔁 duplicate sends if delivery is at-least-once
Why: a reassuring claim often answers a narrower question than the one the reader hears.
items.learnMore:
Read claims for what they do not say

'Retained for 7 days' speaks to bytes surviving. It does not say how many times each event is processed or what a duplicate does to a customer. The review comment asks for the missing guarantee.

Common mistake

Accepting a true but incomplete statement because its wording is technically correct.
items.reflection: Think of a reassuring claim you have heard in daily life, 'it's covered' or 'it's backed up'. What narrower thing might it really have meant?

The event jumps to the front and then stays stuck there
items.explanation: Under at-least-once delivery a crash before recording success causes redelivery, so the second email can be sent.

items.prompt: Why is a missing retry cap blocking while a missing volume estimate is should-fix?
choices: Retry gaps can stall all confirmations; a volume estimate can be added without redesign
The first is simply longer to write about than the second one
Volume estimates are never important to include in any design
Retry caps are the author's personal preference rather than risk
items.explanation: Retry handling threatens every confirmation and must be settled; a volume estimate can be added without changing the design, so it is worth fixing but not gating.
items.reference:
Six comments, sorted
🛑 blocking: repeated-failure handling
🛑 blocking: delivery guarantee and idempotency
🔧 should-fix: rollback plan
🔧 should-fix: expected event volume
❓ question: simpler queue considered?
🪶 nit: two spellings of the service name
Why: a finding is sorted by what it risks, not by how easy it was to notice.
items.learnMore:
Sorting is a judgment about risk

Missing retry limits can stall every confirmation, so it blocks. A missing rollback plan is worth fixing but the design can proceed with a promise to add it, so it is should-fix.

Common mistake

Sorting by the order findings were noticed instead of by the damage they could do.

items.explanation: Severity follows the cost of being wrong.

items.explanation: The stakes are much higher.

items.prompt: The same at-least-once design moves from order emails to payment confirmation. What happens to the idempotency finding?

It becomes a nit because payments are audited later on
It disappears because payments are handled by another team
It drops to a question because the volume is usually low
items.explanation: A duplicate payment event can charge a customer twice, so the same finding becomes a design-level rework rather than a quick fix.
items.reference:
Same design, different stakes
📧 confirmation email: annoyed customer
💳 payment event: possible double charge
📊 analytics counter: slightly off count
⚖️ severity follows the cost of being wrong
Why: severity is a function of what a failure costs, not of the pattern alone.
items.learnMore:
The worked example is a case, not the territory

The same at-least-once pattern with no stated idempotency is a quick fix for emails, a design-level rework for payments, and a question for an internal counter. Reviewing means asking what failure costs here.

Common mistake

Copying last review's severities onto a new doc with the same pattern but different stakes.
